name: Bacama
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.source_named: Carnochan, Jack. 'Bachama and Chadic' (Crossref-verified) and Carnochan 1970 'Categories of the verbal piece in Bachama' (African Language Studies) — phonological/grammatical studies of Bacama; paywalled.
earlier_scan.note: likely tonal (Chadic) rather than stress; no readable stress statement

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid baca1246 and langdoc list (27 refs, incl. Carnochan 1967 BSOAS text, Carnochan 1977 'Bachama and Semito-Hamitic', Skinner & Pweddon 1973 word list, Brønnum 1923 Danish ethnography with 'Sprog' section, Meek 1931)
sources.note: Bibliographic only; none of the remaining entries is a phonological description beyond those listed above; Meek 1931 vol. 1 and Brønnum 1923 are in-copyright and lending-restricted on archive.org.

sources.citation: Gravina, Richard (2014). The Phonology of Proto-Central Chadic. LOT 375, sec. 6.3.3 'Bata and Bachama' (p. 146-147)
sources.note: Bachama section (citing Pweddon & Skinner 2001 and Seibert n.d. 'Bachama word list') covers only palatalization/labialization prosodies; the book explicitly excludes tone and stress from its reconstruction ('though not including tone or stress'). Nothing on Bacama stress.

sources.citation: Kraft, Charles H. (1981). Chadic wordlists. Berlin: Dietrich Reimer — Bacama list as digitised in lexibank/kraftchadic v4.1 (CC-BY-4.0), Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.13832124
sources.note: Wordlist only: 437 Bacama forms, 371 carry grave/acute tone diacritics (e.g. ŋgà fùda ɗìye 'blow', nɔrò 'plait'); no statement about stress.

sources.citation: Carnochan, Jack (1975). Bachama and Chadic. In J. Bynon & T. Bynon (eds.), Hamito-Semitica (proceedings of the 1970 SOAS colloquium), pp. 459-468. The Hague: Mouton. DOI 10.1515/9783111356167.459
sources.note: Comparative (Proto-Chadic consonant correspondences) paper. Marks Bachama words with tone patterns, e.g. p. 460: 'they call themselves ɓwa:re (low-mid tones)... bacama (mid-high-high)... hama bacama (mid-mid-mid-high-high)'; no mention of stress or accent anywhere in the chapter; p. 468 closes: 'the first task is to produce a detailed phonological study of Bachama itself.'

sources.citation: Wama, Gabriel (2020). Understanding nominal and verbal plurality in Ɓwaatye. MA thesis, Theological College of Northern Nigeria, Jos. 48 pp.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Most recent linguistic description by a Nigerian author; theses of this type usually open with a phonology/tone sketch.

sources.citation: Boyd, Raymond (2002). Bata phonology: a reappraisal. München: Lincom Europa (LINCOM Studies in African Linguistics). 60 pp. ISBN 9783895863646.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.access_detail: HathiTrust digitized, search-only (in copyright); interlibrary loan
sources.note: The only modern phonology monograph; per Glottolog/Blench the variety described is mostly Bacama. A 60-page phonology would normally treat tone and any stress/prominence.

sources.citation: Pweddon, Nicholas (with Neil Skinner) (2001). Bwatiye-English Dictionary, with English-Bwatiye index. Jos: Midland Press. xi+188 pp.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Native-speaker dictionary; Glottolog ranks it the language's best phonology-or-text MED; the introduction likely explains tone marking and orthography.

sources.citation: Carnochan, Jack (1977). Bachama and Semito-Hamitic. In P. Newman & R. Ma Newman (eds.), Papers in Chadic linguistics (Leiden colloquium), pp. 21-24. Leiden: Afrika-Studiecentrum.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.note: Short comparative note; only a low chance of a prosodic remark, but it is Carnochan's last published Bachama piece.

sources.citation: Carnochan, Jack (1972). Pitch, tone and intonation in Bachama. Phonetica Pragensia 3: 59-63.
sources.tag: wanted: likely states stress, not held
sources.access_detail: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: The only dedicated study of Bachama pitch/tone/intonation by the language's principal describer; the most likely place for an explicit tone-vs-stress statement.
